expected_title: William J. Levy made eligiblefor reinstatement as clerk in the Treasury Dept. without regard to length of separation from the service. 1913 CSR 132.
page_text:
132 THIRTIETH REPORT OF THE U. S. CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 
October 1, 1913. 
Mr. Leroy E. Reed may be appointed to a competitive classified position in the Department of Justice. 
Mr. Reed has twice passed the stenographer and typewriter examination and held a competitive classified position in the Department of Justice from July 9, 1910, to February 1, 1912, when he accepted a position in the State Department regarded by that department as not subject to the civil-service rules. He was subsequently given a competitive classified status under an Executive order and on April 1, 1913, was 
appointed confidential clerk to the Attorney General. This order is therefore issued to restore Mr. Reed to a competitive classified status in the Department of Justice. 
October 16, 1913. 
Mr. Sam W. Smiley may be reinstated as a clerk in the Railway Mail Service without reference to the period which has elapsed since his separation. Mr. Smiley was severely injured in a wreck in May, 1895, in the line of duty, which necessitated his leaving the service. He applied for reinstatement as soon as he recovered from his injuries but was not reinstated. Itappears that his present physical condition is good. The Civil Service Commission concurs with the Postmaster General in recommend- ing this order. 
October 17, 1918. 
Miss Mary J. Hooff, of the State of Virginia, may be appointed to the position of clerk at $900 per annum in the Department of Commerce without reference to the requirement of examination under the civil-service rules. 
This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of Commerce on account of the character and special fitness of Miss Hooff for this position. 
October 17, 1913. 
Mr. William J. Levy may be reinstated as a clerk in the Treasury Department without compliance with civil-service rules. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury in 
view of Mr. Levy’s former efficient service in the Treasury Department, where he proved to be an exceptionally able and expert technical bookkeeper. His services in that line are especially desired now because of the new accounting system inaugu- rated in that department. The needs of the office of the Treasurer of the United States at the present time are unusual and extraordinary, and Mr. Levy possesses special and peculiar qualifications as a technical bookkeeper. 
October 21, 1913. 
Mr. Monte C. Price may be reinstated in the Postal Service without regard to the length of his separation from the service. Mr. Price entered the Government service as a railway postal clerk August 27, 1886, and was appointed a post-office inspector at $1,200 per annum, with $4 per diem, on October 2, 1893; promoted to $1,400 June 1, 1894; to $1,600 November 1, 1895; both with per diem allowances; and on October 1, 1906, was appointed a city inspector at $2,000 per annum, without per diem. His resignation as an inspector was accepted January 21, 1907, effective January 31, 1907. The chief inspector of the Post Office Department states that Mr. Price’s record as an inspector is good, and that he would not hesitate to recommend his reinstatement. The Postmaster General has no objec- tion to the reinstatement. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend that an order be issued authorizing the reinstatement of Mr. Price. 
October 21, 1913. 
Mrs. Emily C. P. Shepperd may be appointed a clerk in the Treasury Department without compliance with the civil-service rules. This order is issued in view of the long and efficient services in the Treasury Depart- ment of Mrs. Shepperd’s husband who is now confined in St. Elizabeth’s Asylum for the Insane. 
October 22, 1913. 
Mr. Edward W. Cronin may be reinstated in the Railway Mail Service without regard to the length of his separation from the service. r. Cronin was appointed to the Railway Mail Service on August 14, 1901, and retained in the service until March 29, 1902, when he was dropped from the service. His reinstatement is recommended by the Postmaster General, who states that his separation from the service does not appear to have been warranted by the facts. The (Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending that an Executive order 
be issued in this case. :
next_page_text:
EXECUTIVE ORDERS. 133 
October 22, 1913. 
Mrs. Mary R. Geddings may be appointed to a position in the classified service with 
out reference to the requirement of examination under the civil-service rules. Mrs. Geddings is the widow of Surg. Henry D. Geddings, of the Public Health Serv- ice, who was a commissioned medical officer in that service for about 25 years, and who rendered distinguished service in matters relating to sanitation and public health. 
He also rendered valuable service in several epidemics of yellow fever at a time when few medical men were immune to that disease and its cause was but little known. The Secretary of the Treasury states that it would be a fitting testimonial to the serv- ices of Surg. Geddings to waive the civil-service rules to permit the appointment of Mrs. Geddings in the classified service. The Civil Service Commission does not 
recommend that an Executive order be issued in this case. 
October 23, 1913. 
Mr. Henry J. Cokayne may be reinstated as a mail carrier in the Postal Service without regard to the length of his separation from the service. This order is issued for the reason that Mr. Cokayne’s dismissal does not appear to have been warranted by the facts. His reinstatement is recommended by the post- office inspector who made an investigation of the case, and by the First Assistant Postmaster General. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending 
that an Executive order be issued authorizing the reinstatement of Mr. Cokayne. 
October 24, 1913. 
Mr. Solon J. Boughton may be reinstated as assistant examiner in the Patent Office, Department of the Interior, without reference to the period of his separation from the service. Mr. Boughton served as an assistant patent examiner from December 1, 1907, to August 9, 1911. He resigned for the purpose of taking up his residence in Colorado when it was found that he had contracted tuberculosis. A cure was effected within a 
short time and during his period of eligibility he communicated with the Patent Office relative to reinstatement but was ad vised to remain in Colorado and was promised that a recommendation would be made for his reinstatement when he desired to resume his duties. The Secretary of the Interior recommends the reinstatement on account of Mr. Boughton’s experience and the fact that he served with great ability. The Civil 
Service Commission concurs in recommending this Executive order. 
October 29, 1913. 
Mr. John H. Jenkins

William A. Ryan may be appointed to the position of comptroller (in charge of all finances and accounting) in the Reclamation Service. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Interior, with the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission, and is based upon Mr. Ryan’s un- usual qualifications for the position and the close personal relationship which he will bear to the Secretary of the Interior. Mr. Ryan has been in the employ of the Inter- state Commerce Commission during the past six years assigned to the duty of examining the books and accounts of transportation companies, and conducted a notable investi- gation which covered a period of three years. He has been known to the Secre- tary of the Interior for 25 years, and knows his attitude so perfectly that he will be able to state his policies and deal with the more than 20,000 water users without 
embarrassment to the Secretary. 
October 30, 1913. 
Charles J. Brown may be reinstated as a clerk in the classified service of the Treasury Department without observance of the rules regarding reinstatement after the expira- tion of one year from date of separation from the service. This order is recommended by the Secretary of the Treasury in view of Mr. Brown's 
former efficient service in that department.

October 30, 1913. 
Mr. J. Leo Skelly, of New Jersey, may be appointed as automobile expert in the Post Office Department, without reference to the requirement of examination under the civil-service rules. 
This order is issued at the suggestion of the Postmaster General that, owing to the recent purchase of a large number of cars for the parcel-post service, and the fact that Lieut. Herman Kotzschmar, jr., of the Revenue Cutter Service, who has been acting in the capacity of automobile expert for the Post Office Department, has been ordered 
to sea duty, the services of an expert are all the more necessary. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend that an Executive order be issued in this case.

122 THIRTY-FIRST REPORT U. S. CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 
December 5, 1913. 
Mr. Herbert L. Solyom may be reinstated as an assistant examiner in the Patent Office, the year limit upon eligibility in his case being waived. Mr. Solyom served four and one-half years as an assistant examiner in the Patent Office, resigning on August 9, 1907, to accept the position of chief forecaster in the meteorological office of the Argentine Republic. While employed as assistant exam- iner in the Patent Office he displayed unusual ability and scientific attainments, his work being excellent as to quality and quantity. A man of Mr. Solyom’s experience is more valuable than a new appointee would be within three or four years. In view of the technical character of the position of assistant examiner and the evident qualifications of Mr. Solyom for the position, the Civil Service Commission joins with the Secretary of the Interior in recommending an Executive order waiving the year limit, to permit his reinstatement. 
December 10, 1913. 
Mr. George P. Herndon may be appointed to a clerkship in the Bureau of the Census, Department of Commerce, at $1,000 per annum, without reference to the requirement of examination under the civil-service rules. Mr. Herndon was appointed a clerk at $900 per annum in the Bureau of the Census on June 1, 1900; promoted to $1,000 September 1, 1900; and to $1,200 November 15, 1901. His services were discontinued June 30, 1902. This order is issued in view of the satisfactory service rendered by Mr. Herndon in the Twelfth Census and the statement of the Director of the Census that he would be glad to recommend the reinstatement of Mr. Herndon, which the Secretary of Com- merce approves. 
December 18, 1913. 
Mr. Alfred Freeman, of New Jersey, may be appointed clerk in the postal service without reference to the requirement of examination under the civil-service rules. This order is issued at the suggestion of the Postmaster General on account of the great increase in the handling of packages due to the introduction of the parcel post. Mr. Freeman has had more than 12 years’ experience supervising the delivery of small packages and the handling of a large force of men. 
December 22, 1913. 
Mr. Albert K. Brown, now employed as a classified laborer in the Bureau of Fish and Fisheries, may be promoted to the position of clerk at $1,200 per annum without examination under the civil-service rules. Mr. Brown has for years performed without promotion work of a character that would justify much larger pay. This action is taken on account of Mr. Brown’s experience and his admitted intelligence, skill, and exceptional ability for the position for which his promotion is proposed. His promotion is recommended by the Secretary of Commerce, which is concurred in by Mr. Brown’s superiors in the Bureau of Fish and Fisheries. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending 
that an Executive order be issued in this case. 
December 22, 1913. 
Mrs. Mary Hill Dunn may be appointed as a clerk in the Navy Department without compliance with the civil-service rules. Mrs. Dunn is the wife of Mr. Charles A. Dunn, who was employed in the Secretary’s office of the Navy Department for a period of over 23 years, he having resigned March 15, 1909, as clerk at $1,800 per annum, on account of the fact that he was afflicted with tuberculosis. For the greater portion of the period since that date he has been confined at the naval hospital, Las Animas, Colo., and his wife and two small children are without means of support. While employed in the Navy Department Mr. Dunn rendered efficient service, and was considered one of the most valuable clerks in the office. Mrs. Dunn has had considerable experience in office work outside the Gov￾ernment service, and was recently temporarily employed in the Census Office and the Pension Office. The Secretary of the Navy is satisfied that she is well qualified to perform the duties of a clerkship, and recommends that an Executive os be issued authorizing her appointment. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation. 
December 22, 1913. 
Mr. Herbert L. Halter may be appointed a rural carrier at Hershey, Nebr., without reference to the civil-service rules. Mr. Halter was a clerk in the Navy Department from June 19. 1909, to September 27, 1911. His separation was due to his having contracted tuberculosis, and he has
next_page_text:
EXECUTIVE ORDERS. 123 
since received treatment at the naval hospital at Las Animas, Colo. The disease has been arrested, but it is necessary that he remain in a climate which is similar. His appointment as rural carrier was requested by the Secretary of the Navy and is con￾curred in by the Postmaster General and the Civil Service Commission. 
December 22, 1913. 
Miss Anita H. Stephens, formerly an employee in the Philippine civil service, may be appointed to the position of clerk (first grade) in the Department of Commerce, without further examination under the civil-service rules. Miss Stephens was formerly employed in the Library of Congress and was trans- ferred to the position of assistant librarian in the bureau of science at Manila, at an annual compensation of $1,400, the Civil Seivice Commission having certified that she had submitted evidence of her training and experience from which it appeared that she had the requisite qualifications to render her eligible for appointment. In view of the excellent service of Miss Stephens in the Philippines and the fact that the condition of her health made it necessary for her to leave the islands two months before the expiration of the three-year period of service which would have rendered her eligible for transfer this order is issued. The transfer and appointment of Miss Stephens is recommended by the Assistant Secretary of War and the Chief of the Bureau of Insular Affairs, and is concurred in by the Secretary of Commerce. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending that an order be issued in this case. 
January 19, 1914. 
Miss Edith P. Johnson may be continued as chief operator of a billing machine in the office of the appraiser of merchandise at the port of New York without reference to the civil-service rules. Miss Johnson has served in this position since November 16, 1911, and because of her fidelity and industry and certain unusual features of the case, the Civil Service Commission joins with the Treasury Department in recommending this order. 
January 24, 1914. 
Mr. Francis H. Duehay may be appointed superintendent of prisons, Department of Justice, without reference to the civil service rules. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Attorney General, who believes that Mr. Duehay is especially qualified for the position, which requires a peculiar order of talent. The Civil Service Commission concurs in the recommendation. 
January 24, 1914. 
Mrs. Eliza Ryon may

114 THIRTY-THIRD REPORT U. S. CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 
February 10, 1916. 
Mr. Joseph W. Harris may be reinstated as fourth assistant examiner in 
the Patent Office, the year limit of eligibility for reinstatement being waivea 
in his case. Mr. Harris is said by the Secretary of the Interior to have proved 
particularly efficient in cases involving metallurgy and electro chemistry during 
his service of nearly six years in the Patent Office, and to have been contin￾uously engaged in prosecuting applications for patents from his resignation on 
April 3, 1912, to the present time, thus having had an experience of nearly 10 
years in patent work. In view of the technical character of the position and 
the experience of Mr. Harris, and his evident qualifications for the position, 
the commission joins with the Secretary of the Interior in recommending an 
Executive order to permit his reinstatement. 
February 11, 1916. 
Mrs. Annie E. Hudson may be appointed to a position in the classified service 
without reference to the civil-service rules. Mrs. Hudson has passed the age at 
which she would be eligible to take the civil-service examination. She is now 
holding a temporary position in the municipal service of the District of Colum￾bia. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of this 
order. 
February 11, 1916. 
Mr. Monroe Ryles may be appointed as a messenger at $720 per annum in 
the Federal Trade Commission without reference to the civil-service rules. 
This order is issued upon the recommendation of the chairman of the Federal 
Trade Commission, who states that Mr. Ryles is peculiarly qualified for the 
duties to which it is proposed to assign him. The Civil Service Commission 
does not concur in the recommendation. 
February 11, 1916. 
The temporary appointment of Miss Helen Wrenn as clerk in the Bureau of 
Foreign and Domestic Commerce, Department of Commerce, may be made per￾manent without regard to the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon 
recommendation of the Secretary of Commerce, who states that she was cer￾tified for temporary appointment after passing the civil-service examination 
in stenography and typewriting, and that with the exception of a brief period 
she has been serving in the bureau named continuously since April 1, 1915; 
that she is unusually efficient and has shown special aptitude in the per￾formance of the various duties assigned to her; and that it is therefore believed 
that her permanent appointment will prove of very great value to the bureau, 
which is especially in urgent need of competent and trained assistants at this 
time, owing to the extraordinary amount and character of work devolving 
upon it. 
February 21, 1916. 
Executive order No. 2263, of October 26, 1915, authorizing the appointment 
of certain persons who were former employees of the United States Commission 
on Industrial Relations to positions in the competitive classified service without 
reference to the civil-service rules, and amended by Executive order No. 2284, 
of December 14, 1915, is hereby further amended by adding the following 
names: Miss E. M. Green, Mr. Carl Hookstadt. 
February 22, 1916. 
Executive order No. 2306, of February 7, 1916, authorizing the appointment 
of Miss Margaret S. Neate as printer’s assistant in the Bureau of Engraving 
and Printing without certification by the Civil Service Commission, is hereby 
amended to read as follows: Miss Margaret S. Neate may be appointed a 
printer’s assistant in the Bureau of Engraving and Printing or as a skilled 
laborer in the Government Printing Office without certification by the Civil 
Service Commission. Miss Neate passed the examination for printer’s assistant 
in January, 1915, but has not been reached for certification. She is the daughter 
of Dr. John S. Neate, who served for 22 years in the United States Army, and 
rendered most valuable service in fighting yellow fever, submitting himself 
for experiment, and died in 1912 from a disease believed to have been brought 
on by his service. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secre￾tary of the Treasury. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the 
recommendation.

Mr. Edward Rappholt may be reinstated to the position of letter carrier in 
the post office at New York City without regard to the length of his separation 
from the service. Mr. Rappholt was appointed as substitute letter carrier at 
St. Louis, Mo., January 2, 1902; transferred to New York City post office 
August 10, 1908; to the Atlanta, Ga., post office October 16, 1912; and resigned 
December 8, 1912. He made application for reinstatement in December, 1913. 
His application for reinstatement was referred to the postmaster at New York

request for reinstatement in the New York City post office at a time when it 
could have been made in accordance with the civil-service rules was due to a 
local rule rather than to a departmental rule or policy. The Civil Service Com￾mission does not concur in the recommendation. 
February 28, 1916. 
Mrs. Annie K. Campbell, a special agent in the Bureau of the Census, may 
be appointed without examination under the civil-service rules to act as private 
secretary to the Director of the Census. The Secretary of Commerce states 
that Mrs. Campbell has had 20 years of practical business experience, is an 
accomplished stenographer and typewriter, and a trained correspondent, and 
that her experience has covered both commercial work and the technical side 
of manufacturing in both domestic and foreign trade. She has been serving 
since April 5, 1915, as a special agent in connection with the census of manu￾factures, and has had experience in that work both in the field and at the central 
office. In securing her permanent services the Secretary of Commerce states 
that he is sure the department will benefit by her very unusual experience and 
by her exceptional ability. In view of these facts and the exception of private 
secretaries allowed by the civil-service rules to certain other heads of bureaus, 
the commission concurs with the Secretary of Commerce in recommending 
the issuance of this order.

EXECUTIVE ORDERS. 111 
March 21, 1916. 
Mrs. May G. Walker may be appointed to a clerical position in the classified 
service of the Government without compliance with the requirements of the 
Civil Service Commission. This order is issued on the recommendation of the 
Secretary of the Treasury, who states that Mrs. Walker was employed with 
the Federal reserve bank organization committee, and the records show that 
she was graded as one of the best clerks on the staff. Mrs. Walker has also 
had service in the Census Office. 
March 29, 1916. 
Mr. Charles H. Slack may be reinstated to the position of compositor at 50 
cents per hour in the Government Printing Office without reference to the 
period of his separation from the service. Mr. Slack was appointed in the 
Government Printing Office December 3, 1901, and resigned September 23, 1904. 
A certificate was requested for his reinstatement within the year of his eligi￾bility and was issued by this office, but it was returned unused by the Public 
Printer February 27, 1906. 
This order is issued on the recommendation of the Public Printer with the 
concurrence of the Civil Service Commission because of Mr. Slack’s efficiency 
while in the service, and because of the fact that since leaving the service he 
has been continuously engaged in work that would maintain and add to that 
efficiency. 
March 30, 1916. 
Mr. Herbert D. Dean may be reinstated as a fish culturist in the Bureau of 
Fisheries, Department of Commerce, without regard to the length of time he has 
been separated from the service. Mr. Dean entered the service of the Bureau 
of Fisheries in a subordinate capacity in 1884 and in 1891, after four promo￾tions, became a superintendent of station, which position, with the exception of 
five months in 1895, he held until March 11, 1912, when, at his own request, his 
services were discontinued without prejudice. Mr. Dean‘s record was satis￾factory, and he was generally recognized as an efficient fish culturist and super￾intendent. This order is issued upon recommendation of the Secretary of Com￾merce, who is of the opinion that Mr. Dean’s reentrance into the fisheries service 
will be beneficial thereto, and who therefore believes that an exception to the 
one-year limitation in cases of separation from the service imposed by civil￾service Rule IX is justified and advisable. The Civil Service Commission does 
not concur in the recommendation. 
April 3, 1916. 
The minimum-height requirement for the post-office service is hereby waived 
in the case of Pedro D. Mora, an elevator conductor in the State, War, and Navy 
Building, who desires to take the civil-service examination for the position of 
clerk in the postal service. This order is issued upon the recommendation of 
the Chief of Staff of the United States Army, and the statement of the Post￾master General that he has no objection to waiving the minimum-height re￾quirement in this case. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the 
recommendation. 
April 11, 1916. 
Mrs. Mary A. Perry may be reinstated as a printer’s assistant in the Bureau 
of Engraving and Printing without regard to the length of her separation from 
the service. Mrs. Perry, after most satisfactory service, resigned from the 
Bureau of Engraving and Printing on August 23, 1910, to marry. John J. 
Perry, her husband, a plate printer employed in the bureau, died on September 
27, 1915, leaving her with two small children to support. It is also necessary 
for her to contribute to the support of a widowed mother and two minor 
sisters. It is stated that she is 26 years of age, highly skilled in the work of 
many divisions of the bureau, and of a type especially desirable where the 
work is of an exacting mental and physical nature. The Civil Service Com￾mission concurs with the Acting Secretary of the Treasury in recommending 
this order.
